items.statement: Prekindergarten
Number and Operation Sense
Know number names and the count sequence
Count to 20 by ones.
Count backward from 10 by ones.
Identify which number comes just after or just before a given number in the counting sequence to 10.
Identify written numerals 0-10.
Count to tell the number of objects

Use the relationship between numbers and quantities within 10 to count objects with one-to-one correspondence and verbalizing the last number stated is the total when asked "How many…?” (cardinality).
When counting objects within 10, recognize that each successive number name refers to a quantity that is one larger.
Represent a number within 10 by producing a set of objects with concrete materials, drawing pictures, and/or writing numerals. Correctly respond when asked "How many" after counting concrete objects.
Recognize the number of objects in a set without counting (subitizing) with both unfamiliar patterns within 3 and familiar patterns within 5.
Compare quantities

Compare two groups of objects within 10. Identify whether the number of objects in one group is more than, equal to, or less than the number of objects in another group by using one-to-one correspondence, matching, and counting.
Decompose numbers
Decompose numbers less than or equal to 5 in more than one way by using objects, fingers, drawings and/or verbal explanations.
Algebraic Thinking
Understand addition as putting together and adding to and understand subtraction as taking apart and taking from

Represent addition and subtraction situations (presented verbally, without the use of numerals or mathematical symbols) within quantities of 5 with objects, fingers, drawings, sounds (e.g., claps), acting out situations, and/or verbal explanations.
Given a quantity within 5, identify the quantity that must be added to equal 5 using objects, fingers, drawings and/or verbal explanations.
Understand repeating patterns
Identify and extend a repeating pattern (ABAB, AABB, or ABCABC) using concrete objects, shapes, sounds, or movements.
Geometric Reasoning and Measurement
Describe and compare measurable attributes
Describe a measurable attribute of an object, such as length, height, weight, and capacity using appropriate vocabulary (e.g., long, short, tall, heavy, light, wide, narrow).
Directly compare two objects with a measurable attribute in common, using words such as “more/less,” “longer/shorter,” “lighter/heavier,” or “taller/shorter.”
Work with two-dimensional and three-dimensional shapes
Sort two-dimensional shapes (circles, triangles, and rectangles-including a square which is a special rectangle) by like attributes and distinguish between examples and non-examples.
Match and name two-dimensional shapes (circles, triangles, and rectangles- including a square which is a special rectangle) regardless of their orientations or overall size.
Match and sort three-dimensional shapes (cubes, spheres, and cylinders) by like attributes and distinguish between examples and non-examples.
Reasoning with Data and Statistics
Sort objects into categories to represent data
Organize data sets by sorting objects into categories.
Analyze data sets by comparing the categories using words such as more than, less than, and equal to/same (Limit the total in any one category to maximum of 10).
Kindergarten
Number and Operation Sense
Know number names and the count sequence
Count to 100 by ones and by tens.
Count forward from any given number within 100.
Count backwards from any given number within 20.
Write numbers from 0 to 20.
Represent a number of objects with a written numeral within 20 (with 0 representing a count of no objects).
Count to tell the number of objects

Use the relationship between numbers and quantities within 20 to count objects with one-to-one correspondence (arranged in a line, a rectangular array, circle, or as many as 10 things in scatter configuration) and verbalize that the last number stated is the total when asked “How many?” (cardinality).
When counting objects within 20, recognize that each successive number name refers to a quantity that is one larger.
Recognize the number of objects in a set without counting (subitizing) with both unfamiliar patterns within 6 and familiar patterns within 10.
Develop foundations for place value
Understand 10 as a group, collection, or bundle of ten ones called a “ten.”
Compose and decompose numbers from 11 to 19 into ten ones and some further ones by using objects or drawings, and equations (e.g., 13 = 10 + 3).
Describe a given number as one ten and the correct number of ones (e.g., 13 is one ten and three ones).
Compare two quantities within 20 using greater than, equal to, or less than, with objects, location on number paths, and written numerals.
Decompose numbers
Decompose numbers within 10 in more than one way, by using objects or drawings, and record each decomposition with a drawing or equation (e.g., 10 = 4 + 6 and 10 = 4+5 + 1).
Algebraic Thinking
Solve problems involving addition and subtraction

Represent addition and subtraction situations (presented with numerals or mathematical symbols) within 10 with objects, fingers, drawings, sounds (e.g., claps), acting out situations, using verbal explanations, and/or writing expressions and equations.
Solve addition and subtraction problems in context (add to, take from, put together/take apart) within 10 and represent by using objects, drawings, and/or equations.
Understand repeating patterns
Identify, extend, and create repeating patterns (AABAAB, ABCABC, or AABBCC) using concrete objects, drawings, sounds, or movements.
Geometric Reasoning and Measurement
Describe and compare measurable attributes
Describe measurable attributes of an object such as length, height, weight, and capacity using appropriate vocabulary (e.g. long, short, tall, heavy, light, wide, narro full, empty).
Directly compare two objects with a measurable attribute in common, using words such as “greater/less,” “more/fewer,” “longer/shorter,” “lighter/heavier,” or “taller/shorter.”
Order up to 3 objects by a measurable attribute (e.g. greatest to least in height).
Work with two-dimensional and three-dimensional shapes
Describe the relative positions of objects using terms such as above, below, beside, in front of, behind, and next to.

Identify and describe given shapes and shapes of objects in everyday situations including two-dimensional shapes (circle, triangle, rectangle, square, hexagon) and three- dimensional shapes (cone, cube, cylinder, and sphere) regardless of their orientation or overall size.
Identify shapes as two-dimensional (lying in a plane, “flat”) or three-dimensional (“solid”).

Analyze and compare two- and three-dimensional shapes, in different sizes and orientations, using informal language to describe their similarities, differences, parts (e.g., number of sides, edges, and vertices/”corners”) and other attributes (e.g., having sides of equal length).
Draw two dimensional shapes and build or create models of three-dimensional shapes.
Compose simple shapes to form larger shapes (e.g. join two triangles with full sides touching to compose a rectangle).
Reasoning with Data and Statistics
Classify objects into categories to represent data
Organize data by classifying objects into given categories and counting the number of objects in each category (Limit the total in any one category to maximum of 20).
Analyze data sets by ordering the categories by count.
Grade 1
Number and Operation Sense
Extend the count sequence
Count forward and backward within 120.
Count forward and backwards by ones starting with any number.
Skip count forward and backwards by tens.
Read, write numerals, and represent a number of objects with a written numeral within 120.
Understand place value and representations of numbers
Extend understanding of 10 as a group, collection, or bundle of ten ones, called a “ten,” to compose and decompose two-digit numbers.
Compose and decompose two-digit numbers into tens and ones using objects or drawings, and equations (e.g., 10 + 4 = 14; 38 = 30 + 8).
Describe a given number as the correct number of tens and ones (e.g., 14 is one ten and four ones; 38 is three tens and eight ones).
Compose and decompose two-digit numbers in more than one way (e.g. 46 = 41 + 5 or 46 = 23 + 23).
Represent whole numbers as lengths from 0 on a number line (horizontal and vertical) with equally spaced points corresponding to whole numbers.

Compare two numbers within 100 by reasoning about values of tens and ones digits and the location of the numbers on a number line. Record the results of comparisons with the symbols $\gt$, $=$, and $\lt$.
Estimate the location of numbers on a number line by reasoning about their relationship to benchmark numbers (e.g. 10, 50, 100).
Understand and apply properties of operations and the relationship between addition and subtraction
Apply the Commutative Property of Addition and Associative Property of Addition as a strategy to add.
Use the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction to subtract.
Add and subtract within 20
Recall or quickly derive addition and subtraction facts within 20.
Use the count on and count back strategies to add and subtract (e.g., 4 + 1, 7 – 2, etc.).
Use the make ten strategy to add and subtract with combinations of 10 (e.g., 7 + 3, 6 + 4, 10 – 3, 10 – 6, etc.).
Use the ten more and ten less strategies to add and subtract (including those with a difference of 10).
Use the doubles to add and subtract (e.g., 6 + 6 = 12, 14 – 7 = 7, etc.)
Use place value understanding and properties to add and subtract

Add within 100 including adding a two-digit number and a one-digit number and adding a two-digit number and a multiple of 10. Understand that when adding two-digit numbers, tens are added to tens, ones are added to ones, and sometimes it is necessary to compose or decompose a ten.
Use concrete models and drawings to add.
Use counting strategies and strategies based on place value (e.g., partial sums, making tens, etc.) to add.
Use properties of operations, and/or the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction to add.
Represent and explain the calculation by connecting the strategy used to the meaning of addition.
Given a two-digit number, identify 10 more or 10 less than the given number, without having to count, and explain the reasoning used.
Subtract a multiple of 10 from another multiple of 10 within 90.
Use concrete models or drawings to subtract.
Use counting strategies, properties of operations, and/or the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction to subtract.
Represent and explain the calculation by connecting the strategy used to the meaning of subtraction.
Subtract a 1-digit number from a 2-digit number (without regrouping).
Use concrete models or drawings to subtract.
Use counting strategies, properties of operations, and/or the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction to subtract.
Represent and explain the calculation by connecting the strategy used to the meaning of subtraction.
Understand equal parts of a whole

Partition circles and rectangles into equal shares (halves and fourths) recognizing that decomposing into more equal shares creates smaller shares. Determine how many equal shares are needed to make a whole (e.g., two halves).
Algebraic Thinking
Solve problems involving addition and subtraction
Understand the meaning of the equal sign. Determine if equations involving addition and subtraction (on one or both sides of the equal sign) are true or false.

Add and subtract within 20 involving situations of adding to, taking from, putting together, taking apart, and comparing, with unknowns in all positions (result unknown, change unknown, start unknown) by using objects, drawings, and/or equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.
Determine the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation relating three whole numbers (e.g., $8 + \square = 13$; $6 = \square - 2$; $8 + 8 = \square$).
Geometric Reasoning and Measurement
Measure lengths indirectly and by iterative length units
Order three objects by length; compare the lengths of two objects indirectly by using a third object.
Use non-standard units (with no gaps or overlaps) to measure the length of an object to the nearest whole unit.
Reason with shapes and their attributes
Distinguish between defining attributes (e.g., triangles are closed and three-sided) versus non-defining attributes (e.g., color, orientation, overall size).

Compose two-dimensional shapes (rectangles, squares, trapezoids, triangles, half-circles, and quarter-circles) or three-dimensional shapes (cubes, right rectangular prisms, right circular cones, and right circular cylinders) to create a composite shape, and compose new shapes from the composite shape.
Work with time and money

Tell time in hours, half hours, and quarter hours using a digital clock or analog clock. Estimate time intervals (1 hour, 30 minutes, 15 minutes, 1 minute) for activities (e.g., sharpen pencil, soccer game, etc).
Identify and know the value of coins (penny, nickel, dime, and quarter) and bills ($1,$5, $10, and$20).
Reasoning with Data and Statistics
Represent and interpret data
Ask and answer questions by collecting, organizing and summarizing data.
Craft a question that can be answered by collecting categorical data.
Collect and organize categorical data (into up to three categories) using surveys or observations.
Represent data by creating tally charts and picture graphs.
Summarize the data presented in tally charts using “most,” “least,” “greater than,” “less than,” and “equal to”.
Grade 2
Number and Operation Sense
Understand place value and representations of numbers
Use understanding of 100 as a bundle of ten tens, called a “hundred,” and compose and decompose three-digit numbers.
Compose and decompose three-digit numbers into hundreds, tens, and ones by using objects, drawings, and/or equations (e.g., 328 = 300 + 20 + 8 or 328 is thirty-two tens and 8 ones).
Describe a given number as the correct number of hundreds, tens, and ones (e.g., 328 is three hundreds, two tens and eight ones).
Compose and decompose three-digit numbers in more than one way (e.g., 439 = 400 + 39 or 439 = 435 + 4).
Count forward and backward within 1000 starting with any number.
Skip-count forward and backwards by 2s, 5s, 10s, and 100s.
Use skip-counting to find the total number of objects arranged in rectangular arrays with up to 5 rows and up to 5 columns.
Read and write numbers within 1000 using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form.

Compare two numbers within 1000 by reasoning about the values of the hundreds, tens, and ones digits and/or the location of the numbers on a number line. Record the results of comparisons with the symbols $\gt$, $=$, and $\lt$.
Estimate quantities by reasoning about their location on a number line, their relationship to benchmark numbers (e.g. 10, 50, 100), and to assess reasonableness of sums and differences.
Add and subtract within 20
Recall or quickly derive addition and subtraction facts within 20.
Use counting, make ten, and ten more/less, doubling strategies to add and subtract.
Use the use ten strategy (e.g., think of 9 + 1 + 6 to solve 9 + 7) and doubles plus one strategy (e.g., think of 4 + 4 + 1 to solve 4 + 5) to add and subtract.
Use the inverse operation to add and subtract (e.g. think of 7 + ? = 15 to solve 15 – 7 = ?).
Use representations, place value understanding, and properties of operations to add and subtract
Represent whole number sums and differences within 100 using lengths on a number line.
Fluently add and subtract within 100.
Use strategies based on counting (e.g., counting on, counting back) and place value (e.g., partial sums, making tens, etc.) to add and subtract.
Use properties of operations, and the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction to add and subtract.
Determine and explain when a strategy is most efficient.

Add and subtract within 1000, recognizing that when adding or subtracting three-digit numbers, one adds or subtracts hundreds and hundreds, tens and tens, ones and ones; and sometimes it is necessary to compose or decompose tens or hundreds.
Use concrete models or drawings to add and subtract.
Use strategies based on place value (counting on, partial sums, making tens, etc.) to add and subtract.
Use properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction to add and subtract.
Represent and explain the calculation by connecting the strategy used to the meaning of addition and subtraction.
Mentally add and subtract 10 or 100 to a given number 100-900.
Understand equal parts of a whole

Partition circles and rectangles into equal shares (halves, thirds, and fourths) recognizing that equal shares do not need to have the same shape. Determine how many equal shares are needed to make a whole (e.g., three thirds).
Algebraic Thinking
Solve problems involving addition and subtraction

Use addition and subtraction within 100 to solve one-step problems in context involving an unknown in any situation or position by using objects, drawings, and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

Use addition and/or subtraction within 100 to solve two-step problems in context involving any situation or position of an unknown by using objects, drawings, and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.
Recognize patterns in numbers

Determine whether a group of objects within 20 has an odd or even number of members (e.g., by pairing objects or counting them by 2s). Write an equation to express an even number as a sum of two equal addends.
Geometric Reasoning and Measurement
Measure and estimate lengths in standard units
Measure the length of an object to the nearest whole unit by using appropriate tools (e.g., rulers, yardsticks, meter sticks, and measuring tapes).
Measure the length of an object twice using different length units. Compare the two measurements relative to the size of the unit chosen.
Estimate lengths using units of inches, feet, centimeters, and meters.
Measure to determine how much longer one object is than another, expressing the difference in length in terms of a standard-length unit.
Reason with shapes and their attributes
Identify and draw shapes (triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons, and cubes) having specific attributes, such as a given number of angles or a given number of equal faces.

Explain that a line of symmetry for a two-dimensional figure is a line across the figure such that the figure can be folded along the line into matching parts. Identify line- symmetric figures and draw lines of symmetry.
Work with time and money
Tell and represent time to the nearest minute using multiple representations (e.g., digital clocks, analog clocks, number lines).
Estimate and calculate elapsed time to the hour and half hour (e.g. If the school day begins at 8am and ends at 3 pm, the school day lasts 7 hours).
Count mixed sets of coins and bills to solve problems in context (within $20.00) involving bills, quarters, dimes, nickels, and pennies, using$ and ¢ symbols appropriately.
Reasoning with Data and Statistics
Represent and interpret data
Ask and answer questions by collecting, organizing and summarizing data.
Craft a question that can be answered by collecting categorical and numerical data.
Collect and organize data using surveys, making observations, or measuring.
Represent categorical data using picture graphs and bar graphs. Represent numerical data using line plots.
Summarize the data presented in data visualizations using “most,” “least,” “greater than,” “less than,” and “equal to” and determine what questions can be answered with a given data set.
Grade 3
Number and Operation Sense
Understand place value
Apply and extend place value understanding to whole numbers within 10,000.
Read and write whole numbers using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form.
Compose and decompose whole numbers.
Estimate quantities by reasoning about their location on a number line, their relationship to benchmark numbers, and rounding to nearest 10 or 100.
Compare two whole numbers by reasoning about the values of the digits and the location of the numbers on a number line. Record the results of comparisons with the symbols $\gt$, $=$, and $\lt$.
Represent and interpret problems involving multiplication and division
Represent and interpret multiplication of two factors (0- 10) as equal groups or as a composed unit that can be repeated/iterated. Explain the relationship between the factors and products.

Represent and interpret whole-number quotients (0-10) as dividing an amount into known number of groups (partitive) or as dividing an amount into groups of known size (quotative). Explain the relationship between the quotient, divisor, and dividend.
Understand properties of multiplication and the relationship between multiplication and division
Identify and apply the Commutative Property of Multiplication, Associative Property of Multiplication, and Distributive Property of Multiplication as strategies to multiply.

Explain and use the inverse relationship between multiplication and division to determine the unknown whole number in a multiplication or division equation involving three whole numbers (e.g., find 32 ÷ 8 by thinking of unknown-factor problem and finding the number that equals 32 when multiplied by 8).
Use place value understanding and properties of operations to perform multidigit arithmetic
Estimate sums and differences within 1,000 using benchmark numbers and front-end estimation. Determine when an estimate is appropriate and when an exact answer is needed.
Fluently add and subtract within 1,000.
Use computational strategies efficiently (e.g., decomposition, partials sums, compensation, make ten/hundred/thousand) to add and subtract.
Use properties of operations, and/or the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction.
Determine and explain when a strategy is most efficient.
Multiply one-digit whole numbers by multiples of 10 in the range of 10-90 (e.g., 9 × 80;60 × 5) using strategies based on place value and properties of operations.
Multiply and divide within 100
Recall or quickly derive multiplication and division facts within 100 (e.g., factors less than or equal to 10 and quotients less than or equal to 10).
Skip count (2s, 5s, 10s) and apply properties of operations (0s, 1s) to derive foundational facts.
Derive unknown facts from known facts using double facts (e.g., to solve $4 \times 3$, double 3 to get 6 and double 6 to get 12) to multiply and divide.
Use properties of operations (e.g., to solve $8 \times 7$, think of $(5 \times 7) + (3 \times 7)$) to multiply.
Use the inverse relationship between multiplication and division (e.g., think of $4 \times ? = 28$ to solve $28 \div 4 = ?$) to multiply and divide.
Develop understanding of fractions as numbers
Recognize and explain that a fraction represents a part of a whole.
Partition shapes into parts with equal areas and express the area of each part using a unit fraction.
Explain that a fraction $\frac{1}{d}$ represents one part of a whole that is divided into d equal parts, and that a fraction $\frac{c}{d}$ represents c parts of size $\frac{1}{d}$.
Explain a fraction of a set $\frac{c}{d}$ as the quantity formed by c items as part of the given set of d objects.
Represent a fraction as a number on the number line.

Represent a fraction $\frac{c}{d}$ on a number line by defining the interval from 0 to 1 as the whole and partitioning it into d equal lengths. Recognize that each length measures $\frac{1}{d}$ and that the endpoints of the length starting at 0 represents the number $\frac{c}{d}$ on the number line.

Represent a fraction $\frac{c}{d}$ on a number line by marking off c lengths of $\frac{1}{d}$ from 0. Recognize that the resulting interval has size $\frac{c}{d}$ and that the endpoint of the length locates the number $\frac{c}{d}$ on the number line.
Explain equivalence of fractions and compare fractions by reasoning about their size, recognizing that comparisons are valid only when the two fractions refer to the same whole.
Represent two fractions as equivalent if they are the same size, or they represent the same point on the number line.

Identify and generate equivalent fractions (e.g., $\frac{1}{2} = \frac{2}{4}$, $\frac{4}{6} = \frac{2}{3}$) and explain why the fractions are equivalent using concrete materials, drawings, number lines, or equations.

Express whole numbers as fractions, and identify fractions that are equivalent to whole numbers (e.g., express $3$ in the form $3 = \frac{3}{1}$; recognize that $6 = \frac{6}{1}$; locate $\frac{4}{4}$ and $1$ at the same point on a number line).

Compare two fractions with the same numerator or the same denominator by reasoning about their size. Record the results of comparisons with the symbols $\gt$, $=$, or $\lt$, and justify the conclusions (e.g., by using concrete materials, drawings, number lines, and/or equations).
Algebraic Thinking
Solve problems involving the four operations and identify and explain patterns in arithmetic
Use multiplication and division within 100 to solve one- step problems in context involving equal groups, arrays, and area by using concrete materials, drawings, and/or equations.
Use the four operations to solve two-step problems in context (within number limits for each operation as stated in 3.NOS.B and 3.NOS.D).
Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity.
Assess the reasonableness of answers in terms of context, using mental computation and estimation strategies including, rounding, front- end estimation, and benchmark numbers.

Identify arithmetic patterns and explain them using properties of operations (e.g., observe the pattern that 4 times a number is always even and explain why 4 times a number can be decomposed into two equal addends).
Geometric Reasoning and Measurement
Solve problems involving measurement and estimation of intervals of time, liquid, and masses of objects
Measure the length of an object to the nearest half and quarter unit by using appropriate tools (e.g., rulers, yardsticks, meter sticks, and measuring tapes).
Solve problems in context that involve addition and subtraction of time intervals in minutes (e.g., represent and solve using a number line).
Measure and estimate liquid volumes and masses of objects using standard units of liters(l), grams (g), and kilograms (kg).
Add, subtract, multiply, or divide to solve one-step problems in measurement contexts involving masses or volumes that are given in the same units.
Reason with shapes and their attributes

Explain that shapes in different categories (e.g., rhombuses, rectangles, and others) may share attributes (e.g., having four sides), and that the shared attributes can define a larger category of shapes (e.g., quadrilaterals).
Understand concepts of area and perimeter

Identify area as an attribute of a two-dimensional figure and measure area of rectangular space by counting square units (non-standard equal-sized units, square centimeters, square meters, square inches, square feet).
Relate area to multiplication and addition.
Determine the area of a rectangle with whole- number side lengths by tiling and connecting the visual representation to multiplication of the side lengths to solve problems in context.
Use tiling and area models to show that the area of a rectangle with whole number side lengths and c + d is the sum of b × c and b × d, representing the Distributive Property of Multiplication.
Determine the area of composite rectilinear figures by decomposing them into non- overlapping rectangles and adding the areas.
Identify perimeter as an attribute of two-dimensional figures and measure the distance around the outside of figure by counting units or adding lengths.

Solve problems in contexts involving perimeters of polygons, including finding the perimeter given the side lengths, finding an unknown side length, and finding rectangles with the same perimeter and different areas or with the same area and different perimeters.
Reasoning with Data and Statistics
Represent and interpret data
Ask and answer questions by collecting, organizing and summarizing data, recognizing the importance of context when analyzing data.
Create a scaled data visualization (e.g., picture graph, bar graph for categorial data; line plot with fraction units of halves and fourths for numerical data) to display collected or given data.
Summarize data presented in scaled data visualizations (e.g., picture graph, bar graph for categorial data; line plot for numerical data) by describing the story the data is telling.
Identify patterns in the data and evaluate whether these patterns might apply to different contexts or situations.
Grade 4
Number and Operation Sense
Generalize place value understanding for multi-digit whole numbers
Apply and extend place value understanding to multi-step digit whole numbers within 1,000,000.
Read and write multi-digit whole numbers using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form.
Estimate quantities by reasoning about their location on a number line, their relationship to benchmark numbers, and rounding to any place.
Compare two multi-digit numbers by reasoning about the values of the digits and the location of the numbers on a number line. Record the results of comparisons with the symbols $\gt$, $=$, and $\lt$.

Explain that in a multi-digit whole number, a digit in one place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right (e.g., recognize that 700 ÷ 70 = 10 by applying concepts of place value and division).
Use place value understanding and properties of operations to perform multidigit arithmetic
Fluently add and subtract multi-digit whole numbers within 1,000,000.
Apply estimation strategies to estimate sums and differences.
Use computational strategies (e.g., decomposition, partials sums) efficiently.
Use a standard algorithm
Determine and explain when a strategy or algorithm is most efficient.
Extend place value understanding and basic facts to multiply a multi-digit whole number by a multiple of ten.
Multiply a whole number of up to four digits by a one- digit whole number, and multiply two two-digit numbers.
Apply estimation strategies to estimate products.
Use strategies based on place value (e.g., partial products) to multiply.
Use properties of operations (e.g., use doubling and halving strategy to think of 12 × 32 as 6 × 64) to multiply.
Represent and explain the computation by connecting rectangular arrays, area models, and/or equations to the meaning of multiplication.
Divide whole numbers with up to four-digit dividends and one-digit divisors with and without remainders.
Apply estimation strategies to estimate quotients.
Use strategies based on place value (e.g., partial quotients) to divide.
Use properties of operations and/or the inverse relationship between multiplication and division to divide.
Represent and explain the computation by connecting rectangular arrays, area models, and/or equations to the meaning of division.
Gain familiarity with factors and multiples
Recall or quickly derive multiplication and division facts within 100 (e.g., factors less than or equal to 10 and quotients less than or equal to 10).
Skip count (2s, 5s, 10s) and apply properties of operations (0s, 1s) to derive foundational facts.
Derive unknown facts from known facts using double facts (e.g., to solve $4 \times 3$, double 3 to get 6 and double 6 to get 12) to multiply and divide.
Use properties of operations (e.g., to solve $8 \times 7$, think of $(5 \times 7) + (3 \times 7)$) to multiply.
Use the inverse relationship between multiplication and division (e.g., think of $4 \times ? = 28$ to solve $28 \div 4 = ?$) to multiply and divide.
Explain and apply concepts of factors, multiples, and prime and composite numbers for whole numbers in the range of 1-100.
Identify factor pairs for a whole number in the range of 1–100.
Determine whether a given whole number in the range of 1–100 is a multiple of a one-digit number.
Distinguish between factors and multiples and explain how they relate to a given number.
Determine whether a given whole number in the range of 1–100 is prime, composite, or neither.
Extend understanding of fraction equivalence and ordering
Understand and generate equivalent fractions.
Identify and generate equivalent fractions using representations and the Identity Property of Multiplication.
Explain why fractions are equivalent ($\frac{c}{d} = \frac{n \times c}{n \times d}$).
Compare two fractions with different numerators and different denominators, understanding that comparisons are valid only when the two fractions refer to the same whole.
Use benchmark numbers (e.g., $\frac{1}{2}$, 1), common numerators, and common denominators to compare.
Record comparisons with symbols $\gt$, $=$, $\lt$.
Justify comparisons using representations and reasoning.
Build fractions from unit fractions by applying and extending previous understandings of operations on whole numbers

Apply understanding of a fraction $\frac{c}{d}$ with $d \gt 1$ as a sum of unit fractions ($\frac{1}{d}$) to decompose a fraction (including fractions greater than 1) into a sum of fractions with the same denominator in more than one way, recording each decomposition as an equation. Justify decompositions using visual fraction models and equations (e.g., $\frac{3}{8} = \frac{1}{8} + \frac{1}{8} + \frac{1}{8}$ or $\frac{3}{8} = \frac{1}{8} + \frac{2}{8}$ or $2\frac{1}{8} = 1 + 1 + \frac{1}{8}$ or $2\frac{1}{8} = \frac{8}{8} + \frac{8}{8} + \frac{1}{8}$).
Apply and extend previous understanding of addition and subtraction of whole numbers to add and subtract fractions with like denominators.
Understand addition and subtraction of fractions as joining and separating parts referring to the same whole.

Estimate sums and differences by reasoning about benchmark numbers and assess reasonableness of answers (e.g., $\frac{3}{4} + \frac{3}{4}$ will be greater than 1 because both fractions are greater than $\frac{1}{2}$).

Apply and extend whole number addition and subtraction strategies (e.g. counting on, making a whole, partial sums, compensation, properties of operations, the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction) to add and subtract fractions.
Solve problems in context involving addition and subtraction of fractions using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem.
Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication to multiply a fraction by a whole number ($b \times \frac{c}{d}$).
Estimate products by reasoning about benchmark numbers and assess reasonableness of answers (e.g., $4 \times \frac{1}{2}$ will be less than 4 because I have 4 groups of something less than 1).

Coherence - Where students are coming from: - S.ID.A.2: Use statistics appropriate to the shape of the data distribution to compare center (median, mean) and spread (interquartile range, standard deviation) of two or more different data sets. - S.MD.A.1: Define a random variable for a quantity of interest by assigning a numerical value to each event in a sample space; graph the corresponding probability distribution using the same graphical displays as for data distributions. - Where students are going: - S.MD.A.3: Develop a probability distribution for a random variable defined for a sample space in which theoretical probabilities can be calculated; find the expected value. - S.MD.B.5.b: Evaluate and compare strategies based on expected values.

Develop a probability distribution for a random variable defined for a sample space in which theoretical probabilities can be calculated; find the expected value. For example, find the theoretical probability distribution for the number of correct answers obtained by guessing on all five questions of a multiple-choice test where each question has four choices, and find the expected grade under various grading schemes. Clarifications/Examples - Experiment with common real-world probabilities (e.g., playing cards) to calculate and apply expected value. - Explore different approaches to find probabilities of events (short term vs. long term). Coherence - Where students are coming from: - S.MD.A.1: Define a random variable for a quantity of interest by assigning a numerical value to each event in a sample space; graph the corresponding probability distribution using the same graphical displays as for data distributions. - Where students are going: - S.MD.A.4: Develop a probability distribution for a random variable defined for a sample space in which probabilities are assigned empirically; find the expected value.

Develop a probability distribution for a random variable defined for a sample space in which probabilities are assigned empirically; find the expected value. For example, find a current data distribution on the number of TV sets per household in the United States, and calculate the expected number of sets per household. How many TV sets would you expect to find in 100 randomly selected households? Clarifications/Examples - Apply the Data Science Process to: - formulate informed questions. - collect, analyze, and report out on data. - make informed decisions based on probability models. Coherence - Where students are coming from: - S.MD.A.3: Develop a probability distribution for a random variable defined for a sample space in which theoretical probabilities can be calculated; find the expected value. - Where students are going: - S.MD.B: Use probability to evaluate outcomes of decisions.
Use probability to evaluate outcomes of decisions

Weigh the possible outcomes of a decision by assigning probabilities to payoff values and finding expected values. Clarifications/Examples - See S.MD.B.5.a and S.MD.B.5.b. Coherence - Where students are coming from: - 7.SP.C: Investigate chance processes and develop, use, and evaluate probability models. - Where students are going: - S.MD.B: Use probability to evaluate outcomes of decisions.

Find the expected payoff for a game of chance. For example, find the expected winnings from a state lottery ticket or a game at a fast-food restaurant. Clarifications/Examples - Analyze the benefits or drawbacks when weighing a decision based on money or another valuable item that can be numerically quantified. - Interpret expected value as the long-run expected outcome of the variable, considering the probability of each possible outcome. Coherence - Where students are coming from: - 7.SP.C: Investigate chance processes and develop, use, and evaluate probability models. - Where students are going: - S.MD.B: Use probability to evaluate outcomes of decisions.

Evaluate and compare strategies based on expected values. For example, compare a high- deductible versus a low-deductible automobile insurance policy using various, but reasonable, chances of having a minor or a major accident. Clarifications/Examples - Interpretations of expected value should be thought of as what is expected in the long run. - Explore the notion of ‘Monte Carlo Fallacy’ (the mistaken belief that if something happens less frequently than normal, it will happen more often in the future). - Work with various simulation tools such as dice, coins, roulette wheels, spinners, and other simulation tools to assign particular payoffs and costs for play. Coherence - Where students are coming from: - 7.SP.C: Investigate chance processes and develop, use, and evaluate probability models. - Where students are going: - S.MD.B: Use probability to evaluate outcomes of decisions.

Use probabilities to make fair decisions (e.g., drawing by lots, using a random number generator). Clarifications/Examples - Explore the use of different tools to generate random samples and explore the fairness of random selection processes. - Students should be required to simulate events. Focus student attention towards the context of the situation and how this is represented with the chosen tool or simulation. Coherence - Where students are coming from: - S.MD.B.5: Weigh the possible outcomes of a decision by assigning probabilities to payoff values and finding expected values.

Analyze decisions and strategies using probability concepts (e.g., product testing, medical testing, pulling a hockey goalie at the end of a game). Clarifications/Examples - Analyze both cost and benefits in different contextual situations. - Explore negative values occurring when the cost outweighs the benefit in certain situations. Coherence - Where students are coming from: - S.MD.B.5: Weigh the possible outcomes of a decision by assigning probabilities to payoff values and finding expected values.

items.statement: Algebraic Thinking
Look for and make use of structure to rewrite expressions in equivalent forms and reason about their properties
Rewrite and interpret linear and exponential expressions to explain key properties of a relationship.
Interpret components of linear and exponential expressions (e.g., coefficients, constants, bases, and exponents) as single entities and explain their meaning in context.
Rewrite linear and exponential expressions in different equivalent forms to highlight and explain properties of the relationship (e.g., growth or decay rate, initial value, rate of change).
Compare equivalent forms of linear and exponential expressions to determine which is most useful for understanding or solving a problem in context.
Make sense of and solve equations, inequalities, and systems of equations or inequalities
Create and solve one-variable equations, justify the solution process, and interpret the solution(s) in context.
Create linear and exponential equations in one variable to represent relationships between quantities.
Solve linear equations in one variable using flexible and efficient strategies. Justify the solution process using logical steps and explanations. Interpret the meaning of the solution in context.
Solve absolute value equations in one variable where the absolute value expression is isolated on one side of the equation. Justify the solution process and interpret the solution(s) in context.

Solve exponential equations where both sides have comparable exponential expressions, requiring at most two steps to rewrite expressions to the same base, and explain the reasoning using properties of exponents.
Create and solve one-variable inequalities, justify the solution process, and interpret the solutions in context.
Create inequalities in one variable to represent constraints or conditions.

Solve linear inequalities in one variable, including those with variables on both sides, using flexible and efficient strategies. Represent the solution set using a number line and inequality notation.

Solve absolute value inequalities in one variable where the absolute value expression is isolated on one side of the inequality. Represent the solution set using compound inequalities and a number line.
Interpret the meaning of the solution set in the context of the problem, including what values are reasonable within the given situation.
Create linear and exponential equations in two variables, graph them, and use those graphs to represent and solve problems in context.
Create linear and exponential equations in two variables to model relationships, and graph them on the coordinate plane.
Use the understanding that the graph of an equation represents the set of all its solutions to identify solutions, describe patterns, and interpret the relationship between variables.
Create, solve, and analyze systems of two linear equations in two variables in context.
Create systems of linear equations to represent relationships.
Solve systems of linear equations using algebraic methods (i.e., substitution and linear combination).
Approximate or verify solutions to systems of equations by graphing and identifying the point of intersection.
Interpret the meaning of the solution in context.
Create linear inequalities in two variables to represent constraints in context and graph the solution set as a half-plane within the coordinate plane.
Represent and analyze systems of two linear inequalities in two variables in context.
Create systems of linear inequalities in two variables to represent constraints and relationships.
Graph the solution set to a system of linear inequalities as the intersection of the corresponding half-planes.
Interpret the meaning of the solution set in context and determine whether given ordered pairs are solutions to the system.
Model and solve optimization problems using systems of linear inequalities.
Represent contexts involving constraints and an objective to optimize (i.e., maximize or minimize) using a system of linear inequalities.
Graph the feasible region and identify solutions that satisfy all constraints.
Identify and justify the optimal solution(s) based on the objective, and interpret the meaning in context.
Use technology to solve systems of equations consisting of a linear equation and an exponential in two variables and interpret the solution within a given context.
Reason about functions
Identify, represent, and analyze functions in terms of their domain and range.
Determine whether a relationship is a function by verifying that each element of the domain is assigned to exactly one element of the range using tables, graphs, and equations.
Determine whether a function is one-to-one by analyzing tables, graphs, or equations, and justify the reasoning based on the relationship between inputs and outputs.

Use function notation $f(x)$ to evaluate functions for specific input values, x, and describe how the output changes with respect to the input. Interpret the meaning of specific values and patterns in context.
Represent the graph of a function as the set of ordered pairs (x, y) and explain how it illustrates the relationship between domain and range.
Calculate or estimate and interpret the average rate of change over a specified interval of linear and exponential functions presented graphically, symbolically, or in a table.

Compare key properties (i.e., rates of change, intercepts, patterns of growth) of two functions, one linear and one exponential, when each is represented in a different way (i.e., algebraically, graphically, numerically in tables, or by narrative descriptions).
Model with functions
Analyze and model arithmetic and geometric sequences using recursive and explicit representations.
Identify whether a sequence is arithmetic or geometric and create an explicit rule to describe the pattern.
Rewrite a recursive representation of an arithmetic or geometric sequence to an explicit rule.
Model contexts involving arithmetic or geometric patterns using an explicit or recursive rule, and use the rule to solve problems.

Represent functions using tables and graphs, and interpret key features in context. Key features include: domain, intercepts, intervals of increase and decrease, positive and negative values, end behavior, asymptote, and points of transition between pieces.
Analyze linear and exponential functions by identifying patterns in tables and graphs. Distinguish between constant and proportional growth.

Extend the understanding of functions to include piecewise-defined and absolute value functions. Represent them in tables and graphs and explain how absolute value functions can be represented as a specific case of piecewise functions.
Relate key features of a function’s graph and table to the characteristics of a context, and justify the appropriateness of a function model based on that context.
Distinguish between situations that can be modeled with linear functions and with exponential functions.
Given a relationship in context where the rate of change over equal intervals is constant, identify it as linear and create a linear function to model the relationship.

Given a relationship in context where a quantity changes by a constant percent per unit interval relative to another, identify it as exponential and create an exponential function to model the relationship.
Analyze how changes to a function’s input or output affect the graph and its meaning in context.

Identify how replacing $f(x)$ with $f(x + k)$ and $f(x) + k$ changes the graph of a linear, exponential, or absolute value function. Describe the direction of the change and determine the value of k when given a graph.

Explain how changing the input or output of a function affects the quantities represented in context. Use the structure and features of the parent function to justify how these changes impact the initial context.
Find and interpret the inverse of a linear function in context.
Show that a linear function is one-to-one and therefore has an inverse that is also a function.
Find the inverse of a linear function represented with an equation or a table.
Interpret the meaning of the inverse in context as a relationship that maps outputs of the original function back to their corresponding inputs.
Geometric Reasoning
Reason about transformations and congruence
Apply definitions of rotations, reflections, and translations to transform figures and use these transformations to verify congruence.
Describe rotations, reflections, and translations as functions that take points in the plane as inputs and give corresponding points as outputs.
Verify experimentally that rigid transformations preserve distance, angle measure, and parallelism, and use this understanding to justify congruence.
Use the definition of congruence in terms of rigid motions to show that two triangles are congruent if and only if corresponding pairs of sides and corresponding pairs of angles are congruent.
Conjecture about and verify geometric relationships
Apply triangle congruence theorems (SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, HL) to reason logically about geometric diagrams, including verifying congruence and solving for unknown measures.
Understand and apply theorems and criteria for parallel and perpendicular lines.

Use theorems about parallel lines cut by a transversal to identify and apply angle pair relationships, including corresponding, alternate interior, alternate exterior, and consecutive interior angles.

Verify the slope criteria for parallel and perpendicular lines and apply them to solve geometric problems (e.g., determine when lines are parallel or perpendicular and find equations of lines that satisfy given geometric conditions).
Use angle relationships and slope criteria to verify properties of parallelograms.

Use angle relationships from parallel lines and transversals, along with triangle congruence theorems, to verify properties of parallelograms, including congruent opposite sides, congruent opposite angles, and diagonals that bisect each other.
Apply the slope criteria for parallel and perpendicular lines to verify when a quadrilateral is a parallelogram in a coordinate plane.
Reasoning with Data, Statistics, and Probability
Make sense of statistical inquiry
Distinguish between correlation and causation.
Understand and apply statistics as a process for making inferences about population parameters using random samples.
Explain the importance of randomization in selecting samples to ensure unbiased and representative data.
Analyze the representativeness of a sample and its implications for making inferences about the population.
Analyze and interpret how data are represented and used in arguments or reports.
Identify key components of data-based arguments, including claims, visualizations (e.g., graphs, tables), and the statistical language used to support conclusions.
Evaluate the accuracy and effectiveness of visualizations in representing data and supporting a claim or conclusion.
Describe how data were collected and whether the method (e.g., sampling, use of randomization) supports valid conclusions.
Plan statistical investigations.
Formulate statistical questions that can be answered with data.
Determine effective data collection methods that enhance accuracy, validity, and representativeness of the data.
Describe, analyze, and compare data using visual and numerical representations to model situations and draw inferences
Analyze and compare one-variable data visualizations on the real number line to draw conclusions.
Construct and interpret two-way frequency tables to analyze associations between two categorical variables.
Use the tables to decide if events are independent
Use the tables to find joint and marginal probabilities.
Represent data on two quantitative variables on a scatter plot, and describe how the variables are related.
Fit a linear or exponential function to data; use functions fitted to data to solve problems in the context of the data.

Informally assess the fit of a linear or exponential function visually by analyzing the graph and analytically by evaluating the appropriateness of the chosen model in representing the data and context.
Analyze and interpret the key components of linear and exponential models in the context of the data with and without technology.
Interpret slope (rate of change) and the intercept (constant term) of a linear model to describe patterns and relationships in the data.
Analyze the growth factor or average rate of change in exponential models to describe patterns, interpret trends, and make predictions in context.

items.statement: Number and Operation Sense
Reason with rational exponents
Apply the properties of exponents to generate equivalent numerical expressions involving radicals and rational exponents.
Reason about the complex number system
Use the knowledge that $i^2 = -1$ to write complex numbers in standard form, $a + bi$, and use them to represent solutions to quadratics that have no real solutions.
Algebraic Thinking
Look for and make use of structure to rewrite expressions in equivalent forms and reason about their properties
Rewrite and interpret quadratic expressions to explain key properties of a relationship.
Factor quadratic expressions to reveal the zeros of the function, and explain their significance in context.
Complete the square to identify the maximum or minimum value of a relationship and interpret that value in context.
Compare different forms of a quadratic expression (standard, factored, vertex) to determine which form is most useful for interpreting a given situation.
Given a polynomial of degree 3 or higher in factored form, use the Zero Product Property to identify its zeros and sketch a graph of the function.

Add, subtract, and multiply polynomials to rewrite expressions in equivalent forms for clarity, efficiency, or problem-solving applications. Use these operations to represent and analyze polynomial relationships in context. Multiplication of polynomials includes multiplying a binomial and a trinomial.
Make sense of and solve equations and systems of equations
Create and solve quadratic equations in one variable.
Create quadratic equations in one variable to represent relationships between quantities.

Flexibly choose and apply methods to solve quadratic equations based on their initial form (i.e., solve equations by recognizing perfect squares (e.g., $x^2 = 49$), taking square roots, factoring when possible, completing the square, or applying the quadratic formula when necessary). Justify the selected method by reasoning about the structure of the equation and interpret the solution in context when applicable.
Represent complex solutions as $a \pm bi$ for real numbers a and b.
Solve radical equations in one variable that contain a single radical term. Explain why some solutions may be extraneous and justify whether a given solution is valid based on a given context.
Create, solve, and analyze systems consisting of a linear and a quadratic equation in two variables in context.
Create systems consisting of a linear and a quadratic equation to represent relationships.
Solve these systems exactly and approximately using algebraic methods (i.e., substitution), graphical methods, or tables.
Interpret the meaning of the solution(s) in context.
Use technology to solve systems of equations that include a combination of linear, exponential, quadratic, and/or radical equations. Interpret the solution(s) within a given context.
Reason about functions
Calculate or estimate and interpret the average rate of change over a specified interval for exponential, quadratic, and radical functions presented graphically, symbolically or as a table.

Compare properties of two quadratic functions each represented in a different way (algebraically, graphically, numerically in tables, or by narrative descriptions), to analyze differences and similarities between the relationships the functions model.
Analyze and compare the behavior of functions across different families.

Compare linear, quadratic, exponential, polynomial (degree of 3 or higher), and radical functions by analyzing differences in their patterns of change and key characteristics (e.g., symmetry, end behavior). Explain how these differences affect the modeling of various contexts.
Analyze how the number and type of solutions to equations vary across function families and explain how those solutions are represented and interpreted in graphs and equations.
Model with functions
Write a quadratic function to model relationships between quantities given a narrative description, table of values, or graph.
Represent and interpret quadratic functions using tables and graphs and apply them in context.

Create tables and graphs to represent quadratic relationships and identify key features. Key features include: intercepts/zeros, symmetry, intervals of increase and decrease, relative extrema, end behavior, domain (if restricted in context), and range.
Relate key features in the table and graph to characteristics of a context.
Justify the appropriateness of a quadratic model by analyzing trends in the table or graph and explaining how the model’s features support predictions or contextual interpretations.
Find and interpret the inverse of quadratic and exponential functions using algebraic and graphical representations.
Restrict the domain of a quadratic to make it one-to-one and express its inverse as a square root function.
Express the inverse of an exponential function as a logarithmic function and evaluate expressions involving logarithms.
Graph a function and its inverse and analyze features (e.g., domain and range, intercepts, points of intersection) and symmetry across the line y = x.
Interpret the meaning of inverse functions in context.
Represent and interpret higher degree polynomial (degree 3 or higher), and radical functions in context using tables and graphs.

Create tables and graphs to represent higher degree polynomial functions and identify key features. Key features include: intercepts/zeros, symmetry, intervals of increase and decrease, relative extrema, and end behavior.
Create tables and graphs to represent radical functions and identify key features. Key features include: domain restrictions, intercepts, intervals of increase and decrease, and end behavior.
Relate key features of higher-degree polynomial and radical functions to contexts.
Analyze how transformations affect the graph of a polynomial function given in vertex form and interpret their meaning in context.

Identify how the graph of a quadratic function changes when $f(x)$ is replaced by $f(x + k)$, $f(x) + k$, and $kf(x)$ and determine the value of $k$ from the graph. Describe the type of transformation.

Explain the meaning of each transformation by connecting the structure of the transformed function to the quantities it represents (e.g., how changes affect the vertex, direction of opening, and rate of change).
Geometric Reasoning
Reason about transformations and similarity
Describe the effect of dilations on two-dimensional figures using coordinates, including how scale factor and center of dilation impact side lengths and angle measures.
Use similarity transformations to determine and justify triangle similarity.

Determine whether two triangles are similar by identifying a sequence of similarity transformations (rotations, reflections, translations, and dilations) that relates one triangle onto another and aligns corresponding parts.
Justify triangle similarity by explaining how similarity transformations establish that corresponding angles are congruent and corresponding sides are proportional.
Apply properties of similar triangles to solve geometric problems in context.
Use the properties of similarity transformations to establish the AA criterion for two triangles to be similar.
Reason about right triangle relationships
Use similarity of right triangles to explain and define trigonometric ratios (sine, cosine, and tangent) for acute angles as properties of the angles, based on side ratios.
Justify the side length relationships in special right triangles (30°-60°-90° and 45°-45°-90°).
Use geometric reasoning (e.g., dissecting an equilateral triangle or square) to explain why the side length relationships in special right triangles hold.
Describe the consistent ratios of side lengths in these triangles (e.g., $1:1:\sqrt{2}$ and $1:\sqrt{3}:2$), and explain how these ratios relate to the angle measures.
Use trigonometric ratios, the Pythagorean Theorem, and special right triangle relationships to solve right triangles in applied contexts.
Make sense of circles and their properties
Apply similarity to develop and use formulas involving arc length, radian measure, and sector area.
Explain and demonstrate, using similarity, that arc length is proportional to the radius of a circle.
Calculate the radian measure of a central angle as the ratio of arc length to radius.
Apply the formula for the area of a sector using radian measure.
Create the equation of a circle given the center and radius; identify the center and radius of a circle given the equation.
Model with geometry
Use geometric shapes, their measures, and their properties to represent real world objects, and solve related authentic modeling and design problems.

Rearrange geometric formulas to isolate and interpret a quantity of interest in context (e.g., solving for height in a volume formula), using reasoning aligned with solving equations and modeling with mathematics.
Reasoning with Data, Statistics, and Probability
Make sense of statistical inquiry
Evaluate and refine statistical study designs and critically analyze data-based claims to improve the quality and validity of inferences.
Assess the limitations of a sample or study design in terms of bias, randomness, and representativeness.
Propose modifications to sampling methods or data collection strategies to enhance the validity and generalizability of conclusions.
Identify potential sources of bias or misuse in data collection, representation, or modeling.
Recognize when correlation is misused to imply causation.
Describe, analyze, and compare data using visual and numerical representations to model situations and draw inferences
Represent data on two quantitative variables with a scatter plot, and describe how the variables are related.
Fit a quadratic, higher degree polynomial, or radical function to data. Use functions fitted to data to solve problems in the context of the data.

Informally assess the fit of a quadratic, higher degree polynomial, or radical function visually by analyzing the graph and analytically by evaluating the appropriateness of the chosen model in representing the data and context.
Construct and interpret two-way frequency tables to analyze associations between two categorical variables.
Use the tables to decide if events are independent
Approximate conditional probabilities and explain their meaning in context, including the relationship between conditional probability and independence.
